stories.title: Cruz, Phoenix and the Brick That Clicked

content.title: Cruz, Phoenix and the Brick That Clicked

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: The Carpenter in Billund
chapters.text:
When they opened their eyes, the boys were standing in a snowy little village. The houses had pointy roofs, and the air smelled like fresh-cut wood.

A sign on a workshop door said: **BILLUND, DENMARK.**

"Denmark?" whispered Phoenix. "That's really far from home."

"And look," said Cruz, pointing at a calendar on the wall. "It says **1932**. That's almost a hundred years ago!"

Inside the workshop, a man with a kind face and sawdust on his sleeves was sanding a piece of wood. His name was **Ole Kirk Christiansen**, and he was a carpenter. He looked up and smiled.

"Well, hello! Are you two lost?"

"Sort of," said Phoenix. "What are you making?"

Ole sighed. "I used to build houses and furniture. But times are hard right now. Nobody has money to buy big things. So..." He held up a small wooden truck. "I've started making toys. Because even when times are hard, children still need to play."

Cruz and Phoenix looked around. There were wooden yo-yos, wooden trains, and a funny wooden **duck on wheels** that went *quack-clack, quack-clack* when you pulled it along.

"Can we help?" asked Cruz.

"Of course!" laughed Ole. "Every toy maker needs toy testers."

So the boys tested yo-yos. They raced trucks across the floor. Phoenix pulled the wooden duck all around the workshop until everybody was laughing.

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: A Name That Means "Play Well"
chapters.text:
A couple of years later, Ole gathered everyone around a table.

"Our toys need a name," he said. "A special name."

"How about *Super Awesome Toy Company*?" said Cruz.

"How about *Duck Company*?" said Phoenix.

Ole chuckled. "Good ideas! But I've been thinking of two Danish words: **leg godt**. It means **play well**."

He wrote it on a piece of paper. LEG... GODT... and then he squished them together:

**LEGO.**

"LEGO!" shouted the boys. "That's perfect!"

"Play well," Ole said again, nodding. "That's what every child deserves."

And that is how LEGO got its name, in **1934**.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Night of the Fire
chapters.text:
One night, the boys woke up to shouting.

"FIRE! The workshop is on fire!"

Orange flames danced in the dark. Cruz grabbed Phoenix's hand, and they ran outside with everyone else. They watched as the workshop, and all the toys inside, burned away.

In the morning, Ole stood in the ashes. His shoulders were slumped.

Phoenix tugged his sleeve. "Are you going to stop making toys?"

Ole was quiet for a long moment. Then he picked up a burned piece of wood and turned it over in his hands.

"No," he said. "We will build again. And we'll build it even better."

And they did. Cruz carried planks. Phoenix handed out nails. And soon a brand-new, bigger workshop stood right where the old one had been.

"You know what I always say?" said Ole, patting the new wall. "**Only the best is good enough.**"

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Amazing Plastic Machine
chapters.text:
The years flew by like pages in a flip book. Soon it was **1947**, and a huge crate arrived at the workshop.

Inside was a giant, clanking, hissing **machine**.

"What IS that?" asked Cruz.

"It's a plastic-molding machine," said Ole, his eyes sparkling. "You melt plastic, squirt it into a shape, and out pops a toy! It cost a LOT of money. Some people think I'm silly for buying it."

The machine rumbled. **CLUNK. HISSSS. POP!**

Out came a little plastic block with round bumps on top.

Phoenix picked it up. "It's a brick!"

Cruz picked up another one and pressed it on top. It stayed... sort of. "It sits on top," he said. "But if I shake it..." He wiggled his hand. The top brick fell right off. *Plink!*

Ole nodded. "Yes. That's our problem. We call them **Automatic Binding Bricks**, but they don't bind very well. Towers tumble. Castles crumble. Some shops even send them back."

The boys looked at each other. They knew exactly how frustrating a tumbling tower could be.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: Godtfred's Big Idea
chapters.text:
Ole had a son named **Godtfred**, who worked in the toy company too. One day, Godtfred came in waving his arms.

"I was on a boat, talking to a man who buys toys for shops," he said. "And he told me something important: *There's no system in the toy business.* Every toy is just one toy. You play with it, then you're bored."

"So what if," said Godtfred, grabbing a handful of bricks, "every LEGO set could connect to **every other** LEGO set? A house, a car, a fire station, a whole town! You could build anything, and then build it again into something new!"

"Like a LEGO city!" cried Phoenix.

"EXACTLY like a LEGO city!" said Godtfred.

There was just one teeny problem. The bricks still fell apart.

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Tubes That Changed Everything
chapters.text:
Godtfred and his team tried idea after idea. They drew pictures. They built models. They scratched their heads.

Cruz flipped a brick over and looked at the empty hollow underneath. "What if there was something **inside** here," he said, "to hug the bumps on the brick below?"

Godtfred stared at him. Then he grabbed a pencil and drew little round **tubes** inside the bottom of the brick.

They made a new brick with tubes. Phoenix held one brick in each hand, lined them up, and pressed.

**CLICK!**

He pulled. It held. He shook. It held. He turned it upside down and shook it really hard.

**It still held!**

"IT CLICKS!" the boys yelled, jumping up and down. "IT REALLY CLICKS!"

It was **January 28, 1958**, and that was the day LEGO got its special patent for the brick with bumps on top and tubes underneath. It's the very same kind of click that holds your LEGO together today. In fact, a brick made back then can still click onto a brick made this year!

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: The First Kid Builders
chapters.text:
A little boy came running into the workshop. It was Godtfred's son, **Kjeld**.

"Dad! Can I test the new bricks?"

"Of course," said Godtfred. "You're our most important toy tester. And today you have two helpers."

Kjeld looked at Cruz and Phoenix. "Want to build something?"

Did they ever!

The three boys dumped out a mountain of red, white, blue and yellow bricks. They built a house. Then they built a garage for the house. Then a car for the garage. Then a road, a bridge, a tower, and a fire station.

Kjeld tested every single piece. If a brick was too wobbly or a set was too tricky, he told his dad, and his dad fixed it. The grown-ups called it testing. The boys called it **the best job in the whole world.**

Years later, that little boy Kjeld grew up to be the **boss of the whole LEGO company**. And you know what? He never stopped believing that kids are the most important builders of all.

chapters.heading: Chapter 8: A Park Made of Bricks
chapters.text:
Whoooosh! Time zoomed forward again.

Now it was **1968**, and the boys were standing in front of a gate with a giant sign:

**LEGOLAND.**

Inside was a whole world made of LEGO bricks: tiny towns, boats, trains, and even famous buildings from all over the world, built from millions of pieces.

"Somebody built a whole PARK out of bricks!" said Phoenix.

"People were coming to Billund just to see LEGO," explained Godtfred. "So we built them something amazing to see."

The boys ran from model to model, pointing and gasping, until their legs were tired.

chapters.heading: Chapter 9: Little Yellow Friends
chapters.text:
Whoooosh! **1978**.

On a table sat a tiny figure with a smiling yellow face, little claw hands and legs that bent so it could sit down.

"A LEGO person!" said Cruz. "It's a **minifigure**!"

Phoenix made the little figure walk across the table. "Now our LEGO towns have people in them. Firefighters, and police officers, and knights, and astronauts!"

"Every town needs somebody to live in it," said Kjeld with a grin.

chapters.heading: Chapter 10: Home Again
chapters.text:
Suddenly the red brick in Phoenix's pocket began to glow again.

"I think it's time to go home," said Cruz.

Kjeld waved. "Thanks for helping! Remember the rule!"

"PLAY WELL!" shouted the boys together.

**WHOOOOOSH!**

And there they were, back in their own living room, right next to their giant wobbly tower. It was still raining outside. Everything looked the same, but it didn't *feel* the same.

Phoenix picked up a brick and turned it over. He looked at the little round tubes inside.

"A carpenter who never gave up," he said. "A fire that couldn't stop him. A machine that made plastic bricks. And a click that took years to figure out."

"And kids who tested it all," said Cruz, with a big grin. "Kids like us."

The boys got back to building. This time, when the last brick went on top of the tower, it didn't glow.

It just went...

**CLICK.**

And it held.

content.ending_line: Goodnight, Cruz. Goodnight, Phoenix. Play well.

true_facts.text: LEGO began in Billund, Denmark, with a carpenter named Ole Kirk Christiansen, who started making wooden toys in 1932.
The name LEGO comes from the Danish words leg godt, meaning "play well."
The workshop burned down in 1942, and Ole rebuilt it.
Ole's motto was "Only the best is good enough."
LEGO bought a plastic-molding machine in 1947, and early plastic bricks were called Automatic Binding Bricks.
The modern brick with tubes underneath was patented on January 28, 1958.
Kjeld Kirk Kristiansen, Ole's grandson, tested toys as a boy and later ran the company.
LEGOLAND opened in Billund in 1968, and the minifigure arrived in 1978.

stories.topic_input: the history of computer gaming leading all the way to when Roblox was created
stories.topic_label: the history of computer gaming leading all the way to when Roblox was created
stories.title: Lennon and the Lost Levels

content.title: Lennon and the Lost Levels

chapters.heading: Loading...
chapters.text:
It was late on a Friday, and Lennon was supposed to be asleep.

Instead, he was sitting in front of the computer with the volume turned all the way down, testing one last thing in Roblox Studio. Just one more tweak. Then bed. Definitely.

He pressed **Play**.

The screen froze.

Then it flickered. Then the colours drained away until everything was black and green, like the screen of a computer from a really old movie. A blinking cursor appeared in the middle.

```
> HELLO, LENNON.
```

Lennon leaned back. "Okay. That's new."

```
> THE HISTORY OF GAMES IS BREAKING.
> LEVELS ARE BEING DELETED.
> IF THEY DISAPPEAR, YOUR GAMES WILL DISAPPEAR TOO.
> PLAYER ONE REQUIRED. PRESS ENTER TO START.
```

Lennon's finger hovered over the key. Every sensible part of his brain said *go to bed*.

He pressed Enter.

The screen stretched toward him like a giant rubber sheet, wrapped around him, and pulled him in with a sound like a dial-up modem having a sneeze.

**BZZZT-KRRRRSSSHHH-PING!**

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Dot on the Screen (1958)
chapters.text:
Lennon landed on a hard floor in a room full of grown-ups in suits and dresses. Everything was in black and white, and a sign on the wall read:

**BROOKHAVEN NATIONAL LABORATORY: VISITORS' DAY, 1958**

Floating next to his shoulder was a tiny, square, blocky creature made of glowing green pixels. It had two dots for eyes and a line for a mouth.

"Hi!" it squeaked. "I'm Bit. I'm your guide. Also I'm 8-bit, which is a joke you'll understand later."

"Where are we?"

"The very beginning," said Bit. "Look."

In the corner, a crowd of people were queuing, which is not what people usually do at a science laboratory. At the front was a small round screen, about the size of a dinner plate, called an **oscilloscope**. On it, a tiny green dot bounced over a line.

"That's a tennis ball," said Bit. "And that line is the net. A scientist called **William Higinbotham** built this so visitors wouldn't be bored. It's called **Tennis for Two**."

Lennon watched two people twist knobs and press buttons, knocking the dot back and forth. They were grinning like little kids.

"It's just a dot," said Lennon.

"It's just a dot," agreed Bit. "But nobody had ever seen a dot you could *play with* before. People queued for hours."

Suddenly the dot on the screen began to fizz and crackle. It stretched, flickered... and started to fade.

"The deletion's starting!" squeaked Bit. "If this level disappears, every game after it goes too!"

Lennon jumped to the front of the queue. "Excuse me, sorry, emergency, time-travel stuff." He grabbed the controller, twisted the knob, and whacked the fading dot back over the net. Again. And again. With every hit, the dot grew brighter until it was bouncing strongly.

The crowd clapped. The level glowed. A shiny golden coin appeared in the air and dropped into Lennon's hand with a satisfying **ding**.

"One level saved," said Bit. "Hold on tight."

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Spaceship War (1962)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

This time they were in a room at a university called **MIT**. It was filled with a computer so huge it looked like a row of fridges with blinking lights. A group of students were hunched around a round screen, shouting.

On it, two little spaceships were circling a glowing star, firing torpedoes at each other.

"This is **Spacewar!**" said Bit. "A student called **Steve Russell** and his friends made it in their spare time. The computer cost more than a house, and they used it to... well, blast spaceships."

"Honestly? Respect," said Lennon.

"Here's the cool bit," said Bit. "They didn't sell it. They *shared* it. They let other people copy the code, and it spread to computers all over the country. Other people added new ideas, like a star that pulls your ship in with gravity."

"So people were making mods," said Lennon. "In 1962."

"Exactly!"

The screen stuttered. One of the spaceships began to glitch sideways.

"Your turn, Player One," said Bit.

A student slid the controls across. Lennon had never flown a 1962 spaceship before, but he'd played enough games to know one thing: *don't fly into the sun*. He looped around the star, dodged two torpedoes, and fired.

**BOOM.** Pixels everywhere. The students cheered.

**Ding.** Coin number two.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Brown Box (1967 to 1972)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

A basement. Wood panelling. A man with glasses was bent over a box covered in fake wood-effect stickers, surrounded by wires.

"That's **Ralph Baer**," whispered Bit. "Everyone else thinks games belong on giant computers in laboratories. Ralph has a wild idea."

Ralph looked up. "Every home has a television," he said, to nobody in particular. "Millions of them. And all they do is show programmes. What if you could *play* on them?"

"He's talking to himself," whispered Lennon.

"Inventors do that," whispered Bit.

Ralph called his invention the **Brown Box**. A few years later, in **1972**, it went on sale as the **Magnavox Odyssey**, the first video game console you could plug into your TV at home. It was so basic that you had to stick plastic sheets onto the TV screen to add the colours and pictures.

"Wait," said Lennon. "So the graphics were... a sticker?"

"The graphics were a sticker," said Bit proudly.

Lennon helped Ralph hold up a plastic overlay while he tested it. When the white dots moved behind the sticker and turned into a hockey game, Ralph did a small, happy dance.

**Ding.** Coin three.

"People call Ralph the **father of video games**," said Bit. "Now come on. Things are about to get LOUD."

chapters.heading: Level 4: Pong and the Overflowing Quarters (1972)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

Music. Chatter. The smell of chips. They were in a bar in California called **Andy Capp's Tavern**, and in the corner stood a tall wooden cabinet with a screen and the word **PONG** on top.

"A company called **Atari** made this," said Bit. "Its boss, **Nolan Bushnell**, asked an engineer called **Allan Alcorn** to build a simple tennis game as practice. It turned out so fun that they decided to put it in a real bar to see what would happen."

"What happened?"

"Well, a couple of weeks later, the owner rang them up. *Your machine's broken. Come and fix it.*"

Right on cue, the Pong screen went dark. A man with a toolbox marched in. That was Allan. He opened up the machine, and Lennon peered over his shoulder.

The coin box was so stuffed with quarters that it had jammed. Coins spilled out onto the floor like treasure.

Allan stared. "It's not broken," he said slowly. "It's *full*."

Lennon laughed so hard he almost fell over. "It broke because too many people wanted to play it!"

"That," said Bit, "is when the grown-ups realised video games could be a BIG business."

**Ding.** Coin four.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The Arcade Invasion (1978 to 1981)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

Lights. Beeps. Bloops. A whole room packed with glowing cabinets, and kids everywhere with pockets full of coins. It was an **arcade**.

"The golden age," breathed Bit.

In one corner, rows of aliens were marching down a screen, getting faster and faster. That was **Space Invaders**, made in Japan in **1978** by **Tomohiro Nishikado**. It was so popular that people said Japan nearly ran out of the coins needed to play it. That might be a bit of an exaggeration, but it tells you how crazy people were about it.

In another corner, a yellow circle was chomping dots and running away from four ghosts.

"**Pac-Man**!" said Lennon. "I know that one!"

"Made by **Toru Iwatani** in **1980**," said Bit. "He said he got the idea from a pizza with one slice missing. He wanted a game that everyone would enjoy, not just people who liked shooting things."

And in the third corner was a big gorilla throwing barrels at a small man in overalls.

"**Donkey Kong**, **1981**, by a young designer called **Shigeru Miyamoto**," said Bit. "The hero was called *Jumpman*. Guess what name he got later?"

Lennon squinted at the little man in the red cap. "No way. That's **Mario**?"

"That's Mario."

Then all three screens at once began to glitch. The aliens froze. The ghosts turned into static. Donkey Kong's barrels hung in mid-air.

"It's a triple deletion!" squeaked Bit. "You can't save all three at once!"

Lennon looked around the arcade at all the kids watching. Then he climbed onto a stool.

"EVERYBODY!" he shouted. "I need two Space Invaders experts and two Pac-Man pros! I've got Donkey Kong!"

Hands shot up everywhere. Two kids took Space Invaders. Two took Pac-Man. Lennon jumped Jumpman over barrel after barrel, all the way to the top.

All three screens blazed back to life at the same moment. The arcade erupted.

**Ding. Ding. Ding.**

"Teamwork," said Bit. "That's a new trick."

"Multiplayer," corrected Lennon. "Obviously."

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Great Game Crash (1983)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

Wind. Sand. Heat. They were standing in a desert in **New Mexico** at night, next to a rubbish dump.

"Why are we in a bin?" asked Lennon.

"Because of one of the worst things that ever happened to video games," said Bit quietly. "By 1983, loads of companies were rushing out games as fast as they could. Lots of them were boring, rushed or broken. People got fed up and stopped buying them. It was called the **video game crash**."

Bit pointed at a truck tipping thousands of game cartridges into the ground.

"Atari had way too many games nobody wanted, including a famously rubbish one based on the film **E.T.** So they buried them out here in the desert. For years people thought it was just a legend. Then in **2014**, people actually dug them up, and it was true!"

Lennon kicked a bit of sand. "So... games nearly ended?"

"Lots of people thought so," said Bit. "They said video games were just a fad."

"What saved them?"

Bit's pixel face split into a grin. "A plumber."

chapters.heading: Level 7: A Plumber and a Puzzle (1985 to 1989)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

A living room. A grey box on the carpet. A kid about Lennon's age holding a rectangular controller with a red button marked **A** and another marked **B**.

"The **Nintendo Entertainment System**," said Bit. "It arrived in America in **1985** with **Super Mario Bros.**, made by that same Shigeru Miyamoto. Nintendo promised that games would be *good* again, and they were. Mario brought video games back from the dead."

The kid on the carpet ran Mario right, jumped on a mushroom-looking enemy, and bumped a brick. A coin popped out. **Ding!**

Lennon checked his pocket. He had seven coins now.

Then the room shifted, and a new sound filled the air, a catchy tune that Lennon somehow already knew. Coloured blocks were falling down a screen, twisting and slotting into rows.

"**Tetris**," said Bit. "Invented in **1984** in **Moscow** by a computer scientist called **Alexey Pajitnov**, on a computer at work. His colleagues couldn't stop playing it. Then in **1989**, it came packed with a handheld console called the **Game Boy**, and suddenly people were playing it on buses, in cars, and under the covers when they were supposed to be asleep."

Lennon coughed. "No idea what you mean."

chapters.heading: Level 8: The Kids Who Built Things (1989)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

This room was quieter. No arcade machines, just a normal office with a computer running a program called **Interactive Physics**. On the screen, a car made of simple shapes rolled down a ramp, hit a seesaw, and launched a ball across the screen.

"This is my favourite level," said Bit softly. "Meet **David Baszucki** and **Erik Cassel**."

Two men were watching a school class use their program. It was supposed to be for learning science: gravity, speed, crashing things together. Serious stuff.

But the students weren't doing serious stuff. They were building ridiculous machines. Car-launching catapults. Towers made to fall over in the most dramatic way possible. They were laughing, trying things, crashing them and building them again.

"They're not just doing homework," said David, leaning forward. "They're *building* things. And they're having way more fun building than doing what we told them to do."

Erik nodded. "What if there was a place where kids could build anything they wanted... and then everyone else could play it?"

Lennon felt a shiver go all the way down his back. "Wait," he said. "Wait wait wait. Are these the..."

"Keep watching," said Bit.

chapters.heading: Level 9: The Final Level (2004 to 2006)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

Everything around them was made of **blocks**. Grey baseplates stretched out in every direction. Little blocky figures with yellow heads wandered about, building towers and ramps and wobbly houses.

A sign floated in the sky. It read: **DYNABLOCKS**.

"David and Erik started building this in **2004**," said Bit. "At first, they called it DynaBlocks. But they wanted a better name. Something that mixed **robots** and **blocks**..."

The letters in the sky began to shuffle and rearrange themselves.

**ROBLOX.**

"It launched in **2006**," said Bit. "Three years *before* Minecraft, by the way. And David had his own player called **Builderman**."

A blocky figure in a hard hat waved at them from the top of a half-finished tower.

But then the ground rumbled. Cracks of static raced across the baseplate. Blocks began to vanish one by one: *blip, blip, blip*.

"This is it!" shrieked Bit. "The biggest deletion yet! If Roblox goes, everything built on it goes too! Every game! Every obby! Every single thing any kid has ever made!"

Lennon looked at the vanishing blocks. He looked at the seven golden coins in his hand. Then he remembered every level: the dot, the spaceship, the sticker graphics, the overflowing quarters, the arcade kids, the buried cartridges, the plumber, the puzzle, and the students who wouldn't stop building silly machines.

"Bit," he said. "What's been saving the levels this whole time?"

"You playing them?"

"Not just playing," said Lennon. "Every time a level got saved, it's because somebody *made* something new. Tennis for Two. Mods for Spacewar. Ralph's box. That's the whole point. Games don't survive because people play them. They survive because people keep **making** them."

He opened Roblox Studio right there in mid-air. A blank baseplate appeared. He grabbed a block and placed it. Then another. Then a goal. Then a penalty spot.

As he built, the static stopped spreading. Blocks started blinking back into existence, one after another, until the whole world was shining.

The seven golden coins floated out of his hand, spun around him, and fused into one enormous, glowing, blocky trophy.

Builderman climbed down from his tower and gave Lennon a thumbs up.

"Level complete," said Bit, and his pixel eyes looked suspiciously watery. "Game saved."

**BZZZT!**

Lennon was back in his chair. The computer screen showed Roblox Studio, completely normal. The clock said it was very, very late.

He'd almost convinced himself it was a dream when a tiny message appeared in the corner of the screen, in green, blocky letters:

```
> THANKS, PLAYER ONE.
> THE NEXT LEVEL IS YOURS TO BUILD.
```

Lennon grinned, switched off the screen, and finally went to bed.

Tomorrow, he had a game to make.

content.ending_line: Tomorrow, he had a game to make.

true_facts.text: Tennis for Two (1958) was made by William Higinbotham for a visitors' day at Brookhaven National Laboratory, and people queued to play it.
Spacewar! (1962) was made by Steve Russell and friends at MIT and shared freely between computers.
Ralph Baer's "Brown Box" became the Magnavox Odyssey (1972), the first home console. It used plastic overlays stuck on the TV screen.
Pong's first test machine at Andy Capp's Tavern stopped working because its coin box was jammed with quarters.
Space Invaders (1978), Pac-Man (1980) and Donkey Kong (1981) ruled the arcades. Mario started life as Jumpman.
The 1983 video game crash nearly ended the industry. Atari's buried cartridges, including E.T., were dug up in New Mexico in 2014.
The NES and Super Mario Bros. (1985 in America) brought games back.
Tetris was created by Alexey Pajitnov in Moscow in 1984 and became huge on the Game Boy in 1989.
David Baszucki and Erik Cassel made Interactive Physics, and watching kids build wild creations with it inspired Roblox.
Roblox began as DynaBlocks in 2004, was renamed from robots + blocks, and launched in 2006. David's player is Builderman.

content.title: Cruz, Phoenix and the Shark Submarine

chapters.heading: Chapter 1: Grandpa Greenie
chapters.text:
The water outside the window was dark and cold, and bits of ice floated near the top.

Something enormous drifted slowly past the window. It was grey-brown, covered in scratches, and moving *so slowly* it looked like it was half asleep.

It turned one big, cloudy eye toward the submarine.

"Well, well," it said in a deep, creaky voice. "Visitors. I haven't had visitors in about... two hundred years."

The boys pressed their noses to the glass.

"Are you a shark?" asked Phoenix.

"I am a **Greenland shark**," said the creature. "But you can call me **Grandpa Greenie**. Everyone does. Mostly because I'm very, very old."

"How old?" asked Cruz.

Grandpa Greenie thought about it for a long time. Greenland sharks do everything slowly, including thinking.

"About **four hundred years**," he said at last.

"FOUR HUNDRED?!" said both boys.

"Greenland sharks can live longer than any other animal with a backbone," said Grandpa Greenie proudly. "Now then. Your brick told me you want to learn about sharks. And the best way to learn about sharks... is to start at the very beginning. Hold on to your seats."

He swished his tail once. The water swirled, the submarine spun round and round, and the whole ocean went **WHOOOOSH**...

chapters.heading: Chapter 2: Older Than Trees
chapters.text:
When the spinning stopped, the water was warm and green, and the boys could see the sandy bottom.

"Where are we?" asked Cruz.

"Not *where*," said Grandpa Greenie, swimming up beside them. "*When*. We've gone back in time. A **very, very, very long time**. Hundreds of millions of years."

Phoenix looked out at the land above the water. It was bare, rocky and empty.

"There aren't any trees," he said.

"That's right," said Grandpa Greenie. "Trees haven't been invented yet. And dinosaurs? They won't show up for ages."

"So what's here?" asked Cruz.

A little shape zipped past the window. Then another. They had pointy noses and swishy tails.

"**Sharks**," said Grandpa Greenie. "Sharks were swimming in the oceans **before there were trees**, and **long before the dinosaurs**. My great-great-great-great... well, lots and lots of greats... grandparents."

"Sharks are older than DINOSAURS?" said Phoenix.

"Much older," said Grandpa Greenie. "And here's another secret: sharks don't have any bones."

Cruz frowned. "Then how do they stay shark-shaped?"

"Squeeze the end of your nose," said Grandpa Greenie.

Cruz squeezed. It bent and wiggled.

"That bendy stuff is called **cartilage**. It's in your nose and your ears. And a shark's whole skeleton is made of it! It makes sharks light and bendy, so they can twist and turn in the water."

Both boys spent the next minute wiggling their noses and ears and giggling.

chapters.heading: Chapter 3: The Shark With a Table on Its Head
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH!** The submarine spun forward in time.

A funny-looking shark swam up to the window. It had something sticking up from its back that was flat and bristly on top, like a scrubbing brush... or a tiny ironing board.

"What is THAT?" laughed Phoenix.

"That," said Grandpa Greenie, "is **Stethacanthus**. It lived a very long time ago. Scientists still aren't quite sure what the flat part was for. Maybe for showing off!"

"It looks like it's carrying a table," said Cruz.

"And look over there," said Grandpa Greenie.

Another shark swam by. When it opened its mouth, the boys saw that its bottom teeth were curled up in a big **spiral**, like a snail shell made of teeth.

"That's **Helicoprion**," said Grandpa Greenie. "The buzz-saw shark."

"Whoa," said the boys together.

"Sharks have tried out lots of shapes over the years," said Grandpa Greenie. "Some worked. Some were a bit silly. But sharks kept going, and kept changing, for millions and millions of years."

chapters.heading: Chapter 4: The Biggest Shark Ever
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH!**

This time, the water went very, very quiet. All the little fish had swum away to hide.

"Um," said Phoenix. "Why is everybody hiding?"

A shadow slid over the submarine. It kept going. And going. And going. It was so long that it took ages to pass by.

"Boys," whispered Grandpa Greenie. "Meet **Megalodon**."

It was the biggest shark the boys had ever seen, far bigger than a bus. It swam slowly past, not bothering the little yellow submarine at all.

Something small and shiny floated down onto the sand beside them. Cruz used the submarine's LEGO grabber arm to pick it up.

It was a **tooth**. And it was bigger than Cruz's whole hand.

"Megalodon was the biggest shark that ever lived," said Grandpa Greenie. "Those teeth are so strong that people still dig them up today."

"Where is Megalodon now?" asked Phoenix.

"All gone," said Grandpa Greenie. "Megalodon disappeared millions of years ago. The oceans got colder, and its favourite foods became hard to find. But other sharks survived. And one of the biggest surprises is this: sharks even survived the giant disaster that ended the **dinosaurs**!"

"Sharks are TOUGH," said Cruz.

"Sharks are SURVIVORS," said Grandpa Greenie.

chapters.heading: Chapter 5: The Shark Parade
chapters.text:
**WHOOOOSH!**

The submarine popped out of the swirl into a bright blue ocean full of sunlight and coral, all the colours of a LEGO box.

"Welcome," said Grandpa Greenie, "to **today**. There are more than **five hundred** different kinds of sharks in the oceans right now. Let me introduce a few friends."

First came a shark so HUGE that the boys gasped. It was covered in white spots, like someone had flicked paint all over it. It swam with its mouth wide open.

"Is it going to eat us?" squeaked Phoenix.

"The **whale shark**? Oh no," chuckled Grandpa Greenie. "It's the **biggest fish in the whole sea**, but it only eats teeny-tiny food called **plankton**. It just opens its mouth and scoops it up like a giant vacuum cleaner. And every whale shark has its own pattern of spots, like a fingerprint."

Next, a shark swam by with a head shaped like a big flat letter **T**.

"A **hammerhead**!" shouted Cruz.

"With its eyes way out on the sides of its head, it can see almost all the way around," said Grandpa Greenie. "And it has a special superpower. All sharks can feel the tiny bits of electricity that come from animals' bodies. With its wide head, the hammerhead is extra good at it. It can find fish hiding under the sand!"

Then came a shark with stripes, like a tiger.

"The **tiger shark**," said Grandpa Greenie. "It will try eating nearly anything. People have found tyres, tin cans and even car number plates in tiger sharks' tummies!"

"Yuck!" said Phoenix, delighted.

Next, something tiny wiggled right up to the window. It was so small it could fit in Phoenix's hand. And its tummy was **glowing**.

"That's a **dwarf lanternshark**," said Grandpa Greenie. "One of the smallest sharks in the world. It lives deep down where it's dark, so it makes its own light!"

"It's like a nightlight shark," said Phoenix.

And last of all, in a shallow rock pool, a spotty little shark did something amazing. It pushed itself up on its fins and... **walked**.

"Sharks can WALK?!" said Cruz.

"The **epaulette shark** can," said Grandpa Greenie. "It uses its fins like little legs to walk between rock pools when the tide goes out."

chapters.heading: Chapter 6: The Great White
chapters.text:
Finally, out of the deep blue, came a shark the boys knew straight away. It was grey on top, white underneath, and had a big pointy fin.

"A **great white**," whispered Cruz.

The shark swam right up to the window and looked in. Then it opened its mouth. Rows and rows of teeth!

Phoenix held Cruz's hand. But the great white didn't bite. It just swam slowly around the submarine, curious.

"Great whites are amazing hunters," said Grandpa Greenie. "They can smell a tiny drop of blood from very far away. And do you want to know a secret about all those teeth?"

The boys nodded.

"Sharks lose teeth all the time. But whenever a tooth falls out, a new one moves forward to take its place, like a conveyor belt. A shark can have **thousands** of teeth in its lifetime!"

"The Tooth Fairy must be SO busy," said Phoenix.

Grandpa Greenie laughed so hard that bubbles came out of his gills.

"And one more thing," he said, getting serious. "People are often scared of sharks. But sharks almost never want to eat people. People aren't their food. The truth is, sharks are the ones who need looking after. Lots of sharks are in danger because of people fishing too many of them. Sharks help keep the whole ocean healthy. So the ocean needs sharks, and sharks need us to be kind to them."

The great white gave one swish of its tail, almost like a wave goodbye, and disappeared into the blue.

chapters.heading: Chapter 7: Home Again
chapters.text:
The red brick on the submarine's control panel began to glow.

"Time for you to go home," said Grandpa Greenie. "Before your dad finds two empty beds."

"Will we see you again?" asked Phoenix.

"I'm four hundred years old," said Grandpa Greenie with a slow wink. "I'll still be here next time."

**WHOOOOSH!**

And there they were, back on the bedroom floor. The submarine had turned back into a pile of LEGO pieces. The red brick sat quietly on top, like it had never done anything special at all.

But next to it, on the carpet, was something that hadn't been there before.

It was a **tooth**. A big, grey, triangle-shaped tooth.

Cruz picked it up and turned it over in his hands.

"Older than dinosaurs," he said quietly.

"Older than TREES," said Phoenix.

Then the boys looked at each other and grinned. They picked up their LEGO shark, gave it a little swim across the floor, and whispered together:

"Goodnight, Grandpa Greenie."

content.ending_line: Goodnight, Cruz. Goodnight, Phoenix. Swim well.

true_facts.text: Sharks have been around for hundreds of millions of years. They're older than trees and older than the dinosaurs.
Sharks have no bones. Their skeletons are made of cartilage, like your nose and ears.
Stethacanthus was an ancient shark with a flat, brush-topped fin on its back. Helicoprion had a spiral of teeth.
Megalodon was the biggest shark ever. Its teeth could be bigger than a grown-up's hand, and it died out millions of years ago.
Sharks survived the event that ended the dinosaurs.
There are more than 500 kinds of sharks today.
The whale shark is the biggest fish in the sea and eats tiny plankton. Its spots are unique, like fingerprints.
Hammerheads see almost all the way around, and all sharks can sense tiny electric signals from other animals.
Tiger sharks eat almost anything, including rubbish like tyres and number plates.
The dwarf lanternshark is one of the smallest sharks and glows in the dark.
The epaulette shark can walk on its fins.
Greenland sharks can live for hundreds of years, maybe around 400.
Sharks replace their teeth all their lives and can go through thousands.
Sharks rarely bother people, and many shark species need protecting.

stories.title: Lennon and the Lost Levels: The Beautiful Game

content.title: Lennon and the Lost Levels: The Beautiful Game

chapters.heading: Kickoff
chapters.text:
Lennon was in the backyard, long after dinner, practicing penalties against the fence.

Left corner. *Thud.* Right corner. *Thud.* Top corner... *CLANG*, off the gutter.

"Okay, that one doesn't count," he told nobody.

He jogged to get the ball, and that's when he noticed it. The ball was **glowing**, faintly green around the seams, like a screen left on in a dark room.

Then a tiny square of green pixels popped out of the ball like a piece of toast from a toaster.

"PLAYER ONE!" it squeaked. "Long time no see!"

"**Bit?!**" Lennon nearly fell over. "What are you doing in my soccer ball?"

"Emergency," said Bit, bouncing up and down in the air. "Remember how the history of video games started breaking? Well, now it's happening to **soccer**. Somebody's deleting the levels. If they disappear, there's no World Cup, no Messi, no penalty kicks... no soccer at all."

Lennon looked at the ball in his hands. He looked at his cleats. He thought about his team, his coach, and practice on Saturday.

"Nobody," he said slowly, "deletes soccer."

"That's the spirit!" said Bit. "Put the ball down and take one more penalty. Aim for the top corner."

Lennon placed the ball. He took three steps back. He ran up and struck it as sweetly as he'd ever struck anything.

The ball didn't hit the fence. It flew straight through it, and the fence opened like a doorway into a swirling tunnel of green light. Before he could think, Lennon was running after it.

**BZZZT-WHOOSH!**

chapters.heading: Level 1: The Emperor's Game (China, over 2,000 years ago)
chapters.text:
Lennon skidded to a stop on a dusty field. Around him stood rows of soldiers in armor, with banners flapping in the wind. At one end of the field, two tall bamboo poles held up a net... and in the middle of the net was a small round **hole**.

"Where are we?" whispered Lennon.

"**Ancient China**," said Bit. "More than two thousand years ago. And that," he said, pointing at a group of soldiers kicking a ball between them, "is **cuju**. It means *kick ball*. FIFA, the people who run world soccer, say it's the oldest form of the game they know of."

The ball was made of leather, stuffed with feathers and fur. The soldiers were passing it with their feet, chests and shoulders, but never their hands.

"Emperors used it to train soldiers," said Bit. "It kept them fit and quick. Later, it became so popular that even emperors played. There were star players, famous teams and big crowds."

"So they had soccer stars two thousand years ago?"

"They did. Now look."

The net began to fizz. The hole in the middle flickered and started shrinking, *zzt, zzt, zzt*, until it was barely bigger than a fist.

"The deletion!" squeaked Bit. "If nobody scores through that hole before it closes, the level's gone!"

A soldier rolled the feathery ball to Lennon. It was lighter than his ball at home, and wobblier. He juggled it once, twice, three times, then let it drop and hit a clean volley.

The ball flew straight through the tiny hole.

The soldiers roared. The hole grew back to full size. And a shiny golden coin dropped from the sky into Lennon's hand with a very familiar **ding**.

"Oh, I missed that sound," grinned Lennon.

chapters.heading: Level 2: The Game With No Rules (Medieval England)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

The first thing Lennon heard was shouting. Hundreds of voices. The second thing he heard was the thundering of feet.

He looked up just in time to see a gigantic crowd of people charging down a muddy village street straight toward him, pushing, shoving and yelling, all chasing one battered leather ball.

"DUCK!" yelled Bit.

Lennon dove into a hay cart. The crowd stampeded past like a herd of cows.

"What on earth was THAT?" he spluttered, picking straw out of his hair.

"**Mob football**," said Bit. "England, hundreds of years ago. The whole village would play against the next village. The goals could be miles apart! There were no proper rules, no referee, no limit on players, and hardly any rules about kicking people instead of the ball."

A window smashed somewhere down the street. A pig ran past, squealing.

"It got so wild," said Bit, "that kings actually **banned** it. More than once! One king even complained it stopped people from practicing archery."

"But people kept playing?"

"Of course they kept playing," said Bit. "You can't stop people from wanting to kick a ball. In fact, some English towns still play mob football once a year, even today."

The ball came bouncing out of the crowd, straight toward Lennon, and began to flicker.

"Grab it and keep it alive!" squeaked Bit.

Lennon trapped the ball, spun past three farmers and a very confused goose, and kept it moving all the way to the village church, which was one of the goals.

**Ding.** Coin two.

"One thing's clear," panted Lennon. "Soccer really, *really* needs rules."

"Funny you should say that," said Bit.

chapters.heading: Level 3: The Night the Rules Were Written (London, 1863)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

A warm, crowded room in a London pub called the **Freemasons' Tavern**. Men in top hats and huge mustaches were arguing around a table covered in papers.

"It's **1863**," whispered Bit. "Different schools and clubs all play football with different rules. When they meet, they spend half the match arguing. So these men are meeting to agree on **one set of rules for everybody**."

One man stood up and banged the table.

"Carrying the ball in your hands must be banned!"

Another man stood up. "Kicking an opponent in the shins is a proud tradition!"

"It is NOT!" shouted several people.

"That's called **hacking**," Bit whispered. "It's a big argument tonight."

In the end, the people who wanted to carry the ball and keep the hacking walked out. They went off and played their own game, which turned into **rugby**. The ones who stayed started a group called **The Football Association**, and wrote down the rules of what they called **association football**.

"Hang on," said Lennon. "Association football. As-SOC-iation..."

"You got it," said Bit. "Students in England started calling it '**soccer**' for short. That's where the word comes from! Most of the world still calls it football, but America kept the nickname."

Suddenly the pages of the rule book on the table began to fade. The ink was disappearing, line by line.

"The rules are being deleted!"

Lennon grabbed a pen and a fresh sheet of paper. "Okay, gentlemen. Quick vote. No carrying the ball?"

"Aye!"

"No kicking people in the shins?"

A long pause. Then, grumpily: "...aye."

The ink swept back onto the pages. **Ding.** Coin three.

chapters.heading: Level 4: The Goalkeeper From Northern Ireland (1891)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

A small grassy field, gray skies, drizzly rain, and rolling green hills in every direction.

"**Milford**," said Bit, "in **Northern Ireland**."

A tall man in goalkeeper's gloves was pacing up and down, looking very frustrated.

"That's **William McCrum**," said Bit. "He's a goalkeeper, and he's got a problem. Right now, if a defender deliberately trips an attacker right in front of goal, the punishment is just a free kick from where the foul happened. So defenders foul on purpose to stop goals! It's totally unfair."

"So what's his idea?"

William McCrum stopped pacing, marched to a spot twelve yards out from the goal, and stamped his boot into the grass.

"If a player is fouled in front of goal," he announced, "the other team gets one free shot. From here. Just the kicker and the goalkeeper."

Lennon's jaw dropped. "He invented... the **penalty kick**?"

"In **1891**, soccer's rule makers said yes," said Bit. "And ever since, it's been the most nerve-wracking moment in the whole sport."

Lennon thought about practicing penalties against the fence, and about the penalty shootout game he was building at home.

"Mr. McCrum," he said, "I owe you a lot."

The penalty spot began to flicker.

"Only one way to save this level," said Bit.

William McCrum tossed Lennon the ball and stepped into goal, rubbing his gloves together. "Go on, then. Let's see if my idea works."

Lennon placed the ball on the very first penalty spot in history. He took three steps back. He looked left. He hit it right.

The goalkeeper dived the wrong way. The net rippled. *Nets were new too*, Bit mentioned. They had been invented around the same time, so people could stop arguing about whether the ball had gone in.

William McCrum lay in the mud, laughing. "Well," he said. "I suppose it works."

**Ding.** Coin four.

chapters.heading: Level 5: The First World Cup (Uruguay, 1930)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

A gigantic, brand-new stadium in **Montevideo, Uruguay**, packed with tens of thousands of fans waving flags and singing.

"**1930**," said Bit. "The very first **World Cup**. The final is **Uruguay against Argentina**."

The two teams walked out onto the field... and started arguing with the referee.

"What's going on?" asked Lennon.

"They can't agree on which **ball** to use," said Bit. "Each team wants its own ball. So the referee has a solution: one ball for the first half and the other ball for the second half."

"That's the most sensible silly idea I've ever heard," said Lennon.

Argentina's ball went first, and at halftime, Argentina was winning 2–1. Then out came Uruguay's ball for the second half. The crowd sang louder. And Uruguay scored, and scored, and scored again.

**Uruguay 4, Argentina 2.** The first World Cup champions ever.

Right at the final whistle, the golden trophy on its stand started to flicker.

Lennon sprinted over and grabbed hold of it with both hands, not letting go until it stopped glitching. The Uruguay captain gave him a very strange look, then a very big hug.

**Ding.** Coin five.

chapters.heading: Level 6: The Greatest Upset (Brazil, 1950)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

Another World Cup, this time in **Brazil**. On one side stood **England**, one of the best teams in the world. On the other side was a team that almost nobody expected to win anything.

"That's the **United States**," said Bit. "A bunch of part-time players. One of them works as a mailman, and one washes dishes in a restaurant. People are betting England will win by ten."

Lennon cracked his knuckles. "Not on my watch."

For the whole first half, England attacked and attacked. They hit the post. They hit the bar. They didn't score.

Then the USA sent a ball into the box. A player named **Joe Gaetjens** dived forward and flicked it into the net with his head.

**USA 1, England 0.**

And somehow, even though England tried everything, that's how it stayed.

"That's still one of the most famous shocks in World Cup history," said Bit, as the American players jumped on each other. "Newspapers back in England thought there must have been a typo!"

**Ding.** Coin six.

chapters.heading: Level 7: The Stolen Trophy and the Hero Dog (London, 1966)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

This time they were standing in a garden in London, in the dark, next to a small black-and-white dog who was sniffing a hedge very seriously.

"Uh, Bit," said Lennon. "Why are we in a random garden with a dog?"

"Because in **1966**, just before England hosted the World Cup, the **World Cup trophy was stolen**," said Bit. "The police searched everywhere. Nobody could find it."

The dog began to dig and whine at a bundle wrapped in newspaper under the hedge.

"This is **Pickles**," said Bit. "And Pickles is about to become a national hero."

Lennon knelt down and unwrapped the newspaper. Inside was the gleaming golden trophy.

"Good boy, Pickles," said Lennon, scratching the dog's ears. "Seriously. The best boy."

Pickles wagged his tail so hard his whole body wiggled. **Ding.** Coin seven.

"England went on to win that World Cup," said Bit, "and Pickles got a medal and a reward. He was even invited to the celebration party."

chapters.heading: Level 8: Kings and Queens of the Game (1958 to 2022)
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

Now the levels were flashing by faster and faster, like a highlight reel.

**Flash!** A skinny 17-year-old from Brazil was scoring in the 1958 World Cup final and crying tears of joy. "**Pelé**," said Bit. "The only player to win **three** World Cups."

**Flash!** A referee in the 1970 World Cup held up a small yellow card. "The first World Cup with **yellow and red cards**," said Bit. "A referee got the idea while he was stopped at traffic lights. Yellow means careful. Red means STOP."

**Flash!** A stadium full of cheering people in 1920s England, watching a women's team called the **Dick, Kerr Ladies**. "More than **fifty thousand** people came to watch one of their games," said Bit. "Then, in 1921, England's football association banned women's teams from playing at its members' grounds. The ban lasted **fifty years**."

"Fifty YEARS?" said Lennon. "That's so unfair."

"It was," said Bit. "But the women never stopped playing. And look..."

**Flash!** A huge stadium in California in 1999. A U.S. player named **Brandi Chastain** stepped up and scored the winning penalty in the **Women's World Cup** final, and the whole crowd exploded. "The U.S. women's team is one of the most successful teams in the history of the game," said Bit.

**Flash!** A small, quiet Argentine player lifting the World Cup in 2022, after one of the wildest finals ever played. It was 3–3 against France, and then it went to penalties. "**Lionel Messi**," said Bit. "Finally."

Coins rained down, **ding-ding-ding-ding-ding**, until Lennon's pockets were heavy with gold.

chapters.heading: Final Level: The Last Penalty
chapters.text:
**BZZZT!**

Silence.

Lennon was standing on a field he knew. The grass was cut the same way. The lines were painted the same way. The goal had the same slightly bent corner.

It was **his** field. The one where his team played on Saturdays.

But everything around the edges was dissolving into green static. The stands. The trees. The sky.

"This is it," said Bit quietly. "The final deletion. It's trying to wipe out **today**. All of it. Every kid's game, every practice, every backyard penalty. Everything soccer is *now*."

In the middle of the field, on the penalty spot, sat one ball. In goal stood a shimmering figure made of static, arms spread wide, blocking the whole net.

Lennon walked to the ball. His coins began to float out of his pockets and spin around him in a big golden circle.

He thought about the soldiers in China, the muddy village mob, the men in top hats arguing over hacking, and William McCrum stamping a spot into the grass. He thought about the part-time players who beat England, a dog called Pickles, and a woman taking the most important penalty of her life.

"Soccer's over two thousand years old," Lennon said to the static goalkeeper. "Kings tried to ban it. Rules got argued about for decades. People said women couldn't play it. And it's still here."

He placed the ball.

"You know why? Because every single day, somewhere in the world, a kid picks up a ball and plays."

He took three steps back. He looked left. He looked right.

And he hit it **top corner**.

The static goalkeeper dived, but it wasn't even close. The ball smashed into the net, and the whole world **exploded** into color. The trees came back. The stands came back. The sky turned bright blue. And from every direction came the roar of a crowd that sounded like every soccer fan in history cheering at once.

The golden coins spun faster and faster, then fused into one gleaming trophy that dropped into Lennon's hands.

"Level complete," said Bit, and his pixel eyes looked suspiciously watery again. "History saved. Again."

**BZZZT!**

Lennon was standing in his own backyard, holding his own soccer ball. The fence was just a fence again. It was dark, and the kitchen light was on.

He'd almost decided the whole thing was a dream when he looked down at the ball. On one panel, in tiny green pixel letters, a message glowed for just a second before fading away:

```
> NICE PEN, PLAYER ONE.
> SEE YOU AT THE NEXT LEVEL.
```

Lennon grinned, tucked the ball under his arm, and headed inside.

Saturday couldn't come soon enough.

true_facts.text: Cuju, played in ancient China more than 2,000 years ago, is recognized by FIFA as the earliest known form of soccer. The goal was a net with a hole in it.
Mob football in medieval England involved whole villages, and English kings banned it several times. Some towns still play it once a year.
The Football Association was formed in 1863 at the Freemasons' Tavern in London. The argument over carrying the ball and hacking helped split soccer from rugby.
The word "soccer" comes from "association football."
William McCrum, a goalkeeper from Milford in Northern Ireland, invented the penalty kick, which became part of the rules in 1891. Goal nets arrived around the same time.
The first World Cup was in Uruguay in 1930. The two teams in the final used a different ball in each half, and Uruguay beat Argentina 4–2.
In 1950, the USA beat England 1–0 thanks to a goal by Joe Gaetjens, one of the biggest upsets ever.
In 1966, the stolen World Cup trophy was found under a hedge in London by a dog named Pickles.
Pelé won three World Cups, the first when he was just 17.
Yellow and red cards were first used at a World Cup in 1970. The idea came from traffic lights.
The Dick, Kerr Ladies drew crowds of more than 50,000, before women were banned from England's FA grounds for 50 years.
Brandi Chastain scored the winning penalty for the USA in the 1999 Women's World Cup final.
Lionel Messi and Argentina won the 2022 World Cup on penalties after a 3–3 final against France.
